html: So, slide 29, Brian. You figure out all the things that are wrong, and then you focus on them with single-pointed concentration. You are so focused on the wrong thing, on the negativity. Jealousy — he says jealousy is your enemy. This guy's jealous of this other guy. He wants the girl; the other guy's got her, and now he's jealous. Why can't I get that person? I'm terrible. No one loves me. Of course they don't love me. Listen to the stories that go on in your mind once the jealousy starts.

Someone was telling me the other day that they use their jealousy and turn it into pride. They're jealous of the person, and they're like, yeah, but at least I have Dharma. I almost fell off my chair laughing. It was so funny. Like, I'm jealous — they have more money than I do, so jealous. Yeah, but my girlfriend's really hot. What? That makes no — what? You just turned your jealousy into two bad seeds. Instead of rejoicing that somebody has a lot of money, you're like, well, yeah, at least my partner's hotter than yours, at least I have that. And then you turn it into pride.

Or, as I said, the best one is: wow, that person's so successful — but I have seeds. I know four steps. Has anyone ever said that? I'm looking at some of your faces — I think I'm catching you in your guilt. You're like, my life is suffering, yours is better than mine, but I have seeds and you don't. Oh, nice. Shut up. But that's what happens. And that's what Shantideva is saying — we anti-rejoice. We even use our Dharma practice to anti-rejoice, to make ourselves better than other people. We say, well, it's 10:30 at night on a Sunday in Taipei and we're learning ACI 17 — we're better than everybody else. I think it's cool that it's Sunday night and you're all still awake. I'm trying to stay awake, and I'm the one talking.

But anti-rejoice — look at your life. And this was Shantideva saying, look at your life and really evaluate: am I really rejoicing, or am I just one of those anti-rejoicers? That is one of the hugest obstacles to any kind of success — your worldly success and your spiritual success. If you're wondering why your good seeds aren't ripening the way you want them to, just get a journal out and call it anti-rejoicing. Every time you anti-rejoice, just write in it. On the other side, every time you rejoice, write in it. Watch the anti-rejoicing list get longer and longer and longer. But I'm serious — keep track of it. Not in the way of, so then you can think about it more. Like, I'm going to be so jealous of all those partners out there — but I have Dharma. Yeah, if I had Dharma, then A, I wouldn't be jealous, and secondly, I would know how to create a partner, and I would have done it already if I was actually doing it, instead of whining about how everyone else's relationship is so good and mine's not that good. Get it? We're insane. It's fun though.
Dedicating your seeds

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: And then, slide 31. We skipped over a couple of things, but I want to talk a little bit about dedication. What are we dedicating? There's this whole idea where oftentimes we'll say at the end of a class, dedicate the good karma. Give the good karma away. What does that mean? How do you give the good karma away when — literally, we tell you, you can't do that? Because if someone could give you the seeds, they would have already done it for you — there would be an infinitely compassionate being who would have done it for you, made you not suffer. If a Buddha could give you their seeds, they would have. What's the proof that they didn't? Oh yeah — butt masks. The fact that you're worried about your aging butt, and that they sell a product that helps it — that's the reason why a Buddha can't give you seeds. But so — just kidding.

And we talk about dedicating our seeds. What does that mean? What it mainly means is that when we do a good deed, we're then trying to direct it toward a result that we want to see. Sure — I need some money, so I'm going to go give some money to somebody else, I'm going to help somebody in a four-step plan. Great. That's one way of doing it. But then when you think about the seed afterward and you do a dedication — one, you're rejoicing in it, you're adding more power to it. And then you're guiding it. You're basically adding more time to it, adding more fertilizer to it. But if you start thinking about it like a bodhisattva: well, I really wish that everybody had all the money they needed in the world and no one would have to do a four-step plan anyway. May this seed serve to be the seed that ends the need for people to get money. May this seed serve to become the seed that will then push me over into my total enlightenment, so that I could really help everyone.

So you're basically taking the seeds and you're guiding them. You're guiding their energy. You're not giving them away to other people — if I could, I would, and if someone else could have, they would have. But you're guiding it, you're dedicating it, you're offering it. You're doing something with — take the most banal thing (translators, here's a new word: banal) — the most normal of the normal thing that you do on a daily basis, like brushing your teeth. And if you know how to dedicate properly, you can use those seeds to help accelerate your path to total enlightenment. Just blinking. Eating. The way you walk. Can you walk in a way that's planting seeds for other people?

I was walking down the street today and there were all these people, and there was just this energy. There's the energy of a city, but there was this particularly busy, stressful area. And I was like, I'm going to walk slow, and relaxed. I'm going to breathe deeply, like I'm walking on a beach — for others. So even each step, each gesture, can be a seed for something greater than just the movement of my hand, or the scratching of the itch on my head, or the drinking of the water. And so you can transform all of those things. And what Shantideva is offering us is a way to do that. Don't waste your opportunities. Everyone thought he was just pooping, sleeping, and eating. But maybe he knew the secret to dedicating all of his actions — even the most banal ones, the most boring things. Could you eat, sleep, and poop your way to total enlightenment? That's a good t-shirt.
Becoming what all beings need

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: But what are we wishing for? What are we wishing for ourselves? We're wishing that we can become enlightened through our good deeds. So that we can become something — we can become the medicine for those that are sick, we can become the cure, we can become the physician, we can become the food and drink that people need, we can become the very things that people and all beings wish for — in a temporary sense, and in an ultimate sense. To be what people need to bring themselves to peace, to comfort, and eventually to a place where they can arrive at that ultimate peace. So be that for those people. When I was walking down the street, I was like, well, maybe I can be that. Maybe I can be that relaxation for them, because of the stress or whatever was happening. I don't know if anybody watched me — I wasn't paying attention, I wasn't focused on whether they were or not, or whether I was helping them. But what if I was also imagining — what if everyone was walking around Taipei like this? That would be a totally different city. And so those are the things you can do. I was just walking from a cafe back to the hotel. You can take a normal walk and turn it into something much greater. And then of course you can do a little bit more and be like, well, who are all those people? And they could be Buddhas, and all that stuff too. And so, in doing so — because I had a little special moment — I ended up buying new shoes. I'll tell you that story later. But they're great shoes. All right, let's move on.
Motivations for the wish for enlightenment

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: Here's some motivation that Shantideva gives us now. Now that we're kind of feeling like — I don't know if you're feeling it, I'm feeling it — like, wow, I could do this wish for enlightenment thing. I could try. We're not going to be perfect at it, we're going to make mistakes. Don't worry when we do. But here's some motivations that he gives us. Once we get there, there's this feeling that arises. So, slide four — oh, you're already on it.

Our lives become more fruitful. It becomes more exciting. The boring walk between the cafe and the hotel became exciting. And it was really fun, actually — I told you I ended up buying new shoes. I've needed new shoes, and they just appeared, and they appeared because of a whole series of attitudes that I think I was having in that moment. Helping people. And then some guy helped me buy my new shoes. It was great. I haven't met anyone in Taipei that speaks that good English. It was amazing. And he's never left Taipei — that was the weird thing. I was like, where did you learn English? And he's like, I've lived here all my life and I sell shoes.

So your life becomes fruitful. Next slide. Second, we celebrate that we've truly achieved a human life. Most of us don't think about this. Most of us don't spend the time thinking, I'm so happy I'm human. You don't go, wow, I'm so happy I'm not a cat, or I'm so happy I'm not a dog, or I'm not an earthworm. Sometimes you do, but we don't think about how great it is to be human — because those other forms of life don't have the capacity to do this. Yet.

What's next? Well, this is what happens when you take your bodhisattva vows — you become part of the family of the Buddhas. Yeah, they are sitting around the table. This was AI three years ago; much better now. Next slide. There it is, Brian. It's a family of Buddhas. This is when AI didn't understand really what you meant. But it was cute. How much has changed in three years is pretty amazing.

And then the next one is that we've become a child of the Buddhas. We are on our way. Why does Shantideva give us all these different points of view? Because some days, to think that you're the child of a Buddha is motivating. But other days you have different seeds and it may not be. So in that sense, grab onto the ones that are meaningful to you now — but then they might change next week, or they might change in a couple of days. Or if you go through a rough period, you might think, I don't know about this bodhisattva thing. I've been in those places several times. It's been 16, 17 years since I met Geshe Michael, something like that. I've had my dark days, dark periods. And then I've had to pull myself out, and having all these different nuggets to pull from — one of them —

If the Buddhas understand us completely, they understand what we're going to need at all the different phases. It's all there. And the more you study this, the more you get this weird suspicion that that might be true — that they've been speaking to us all the time, and they're just dropping the things we need to know as we go along. It's like the breadcrumbs are already there; we just weren't paying attention at first. But once you start paying attention, it gets very suspicious.
What the wish for enlightenment destroys

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: So, what are the different things that the wish for total enlightenment does for you? What does it remove for you? Next slide. It eventually destroys the lord of death. That's cool. This is the wheel of life. It destroys that constant cycle of death, in-between, and rebirth. Eventually. That's cool.

Next slide. It destroys poverty within all living beings. We'll talk about this in a second — this is the question that comes up later on: does the perfection of giving mean that everyone gets what they want, and then poverty is eradicated? We'll talk about that in a second.

It destroys illness. Next slide. I'm not going to comment on all these; I will never get through everything. Next slide. It destroys the general suffering of the cycle of life — just the going around. And more specifically, last slide, it destroys the suffering of the lower realms. That's what your wish does. That's the power of that — to be able to end this.

So, next slide. The question that comes up is, how? The more I look at this — god, these teachers are weird-looking. How do they remove these sufferings? How does the wish do it? As we said earlier, it's not by, "I wish I could just give you my seeds," like the Buddha just throwing their seeds out, throwing diamonds out, and everyone just picking them up. It's more that what a Buddha can do is they can look at you and know what to say, and what to do, and what to teach, that can help you do it yourself. That's how they do it. When you know all things — when you have that omniscience — what does the omniscience do for you? Knowing all things is, you know what to say. You know what can help somebody. And if you have omniscience about past, present, and future, the things that you're saying now, you also know are going to be affecting the beings in the future too. So you're speaking not for now, you're speaking for them as well. And that's pretty cool.

And then it flips it around, and you get to think: well, if that's true, then they knew that we were having this class right now. They knew what we were going to meet. They knew, when they spoke 2,500 years ago, that what they said would be coming out right now. They knew that we'd be on Zoom, that we'd all be looking at each other's faces. And that Shantideva would have his "Mr. Three Thoughts" thing, and then he would have written the book, and then we would be talking about it — what, 1,500 years later, 1,400 years later? So in a way, were those messages for us? If you believe that a Buddha exists, then what they said before was for us right now. And they were like, I know what's going to help you, even when it's 10:45 at night and your eyes are just trying to stay awake. They're all falling asleep here; I've got to tell some jokes or something. But really, if you get into that suspicion, it also changes the way that the seeds are planted, as Shantideva would say.
